utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good morning, everyone. Would the witness take the solemn declaration, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm saying that I will speak the truth and the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, ma'am.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please make yourself comfortable. Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Excellencies. Good morning to all.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Madam. Could I kindly ask you to tell us what your name is, and you can also tell us where and when you were born.

utterances.speaker: ANGELINA PIKULIC
utterances.text: I am Angelina Pikulic. I was born in Podlugovi. I was born in Podlugovi on the 28th of April, that's when I was born. I was born in 1946.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Podlugovi is about 15 or 20 kilometres away from Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: ANGELINA PIKULIC
utterances.text: I know that. I was born there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I know that you know, but I wanted the participants in these proceedings to know that you are from the area. Where did you live before the war?

utterances.speaker: ANGELINA PIKULIC
utterances.text: I lived in Pofalici close to the tobacco factory. Umska [phoen], that was the name of the street.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Where did you work? Did you have a job before the war?

utterances.speaker: ANGELINA PIKULIC
utterances.text: Yes, in the government, the Executive Council. I worked there as a cleaner.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Could I kindly ask you to pause before you answer so that this can be interpreted?

utterances.speaker: ANGELINA PIKULIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You said the Executive Council. Did you work in the Presidency as well?

utterances.speaker: ANGELINA PIKULIC
utterances.text: Yes, in the Presidency too at Milenka Renovica's.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you work after the elections in 1990 and did you know any of the office-holders?

utterances.speaker: ANGELINA PIKULIC
utterances.text: In 1990? Yes, I knew our people who worked at the Executive Council. As for the others, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Until when did you work at the Executive Council?

utterances.speaker: ANGELINA PIKULIC
utterances.text: Until 1979. I got a disability pension because I had an accident on the job. I broke my spine. I had an operation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. When the war broke out, did you remain in Sarajevo in the area under Muslim control, or rather, where were you when the war broke out and how long were you there?

utterances.speaker: ANGELINA PIKULIC
utterances.text: In 1992 and 1991 -- well, that's it, 1991 and 1992. And then war broke out. They were preparing in 1991. And then they started in 1992, in April. My husband was out there in hospital. I went to see him at the hospital twice and they put these things, whatever they're called. There was that military police of theirs. And I couldn't get into the hospital to see my husband until I showed my ID.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. What happened in 1993? Did you visit the Presidency building and how come that happened?

utterances.speaker: ANGELINA PIKULIC
utterances.text: Well, I went to look for food.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you know someone at the Presidency and is that why you went to the Presidency?

utterances.speaker: ANGELINA PIKULIC
utterances.text: Well, yes, I did and these people were not there at all. I was just looking for this man and they didn't answer and I was near the reception desk, where the reception desk is at this Executive Council of ours. So I stood there and I heard this screaming in this one room and in this room -- I mean, was it these Serbs of ours? And I just heard this screaming and this man opened the door and I just saw this man naked, covered in blood.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us exactly what it was that you saw?

utterances.speaker: ANGELINA PIKULIC
utterances.text: I saw this man's -- I heard this screaming, actually, and then this soldier opened the door and then one of them was naked and then the other one was covered with this green thing, whatever you call it, like a cloth. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Why was the one screaming and the other one naked?

utterances.speaker: ANGELINA PIKULIC
utterances.text: I don't know. As soon as I saw that, I started running away towards the mosque. You know where that is, don't you? You know where the Presidency is. You know where the main entrance is, and then it goes towards the mosque, you know; and then by the military hospital and then I went to my home.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Were they alive?

utterances.speaker: ANGELINA PIKULIC
utterances.text: I don't know. I don't know whether they were alive.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Were you arrested or detained while you were --

utterances.speaker: ANGELINA PIKULIC
utterances.text: In Pofalici. They made me go to Velesici.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So you were arrested. And then you were kept where?

utterances.speaker: ANGELINA PIKULIC
utterances.text: In Velesici, closer to the station up there, the railway station.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, in light of the ruling the Chamber has made in its decision, I would like you to move on to your next topic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Excellency, it's linked to what the lady saw there. That is of relevance to us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It has to do with paragraph 10, the one that you have admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So what was it that you saw there while you were detained in Velesici? What did you hear?

utterances.speaker: ANGELINA PIKULIC
utterances.text: My husband, who was sick, was there. He was released from hospital. They let him go on the 15th of April from Gezero [phoen]. Do you know what that is? It's that -- he was released from hospital because he had this thing called gangrene.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. What did you see or what did you hear as far as military affairs are concerned in Velesici? Did you see something, did you hear something?

utterances.speaker: ANGELINA PIKULIC
utterances.text: Well, they immediately took us - my husband and myself - they took us to this room to question both of us. I saw that there were quite a few soldiers there. I don't know. I don't know. I saw all of that in Velesici. They were questioning my husband. They were asking him something, and I was sitting there in this other chair and he was talking to them and then this soldier got up and slapped him on the face twice.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Whose soldiers were they?

utterances.speaker: ANGELINA PIKULIC
utterances.text: Alija's, not mine.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you hear some shooting or something from there?

utterances.speaker: ANGELINA PIKULIC
utterances.text: Well, I did hear something, but of course we didn't dare go out, I mean out of that house where I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Could you tell the Trial Chamber what it was that you heard and what it was that was happening near that building?

utterances.speaker: ANGELINA PIKULIC
utterances.text: Well, these soldiers were there and the people who were there too, Serbs. There were Serbs there in Velesici.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you hear any kind of gun-fire?

utterances.speaker: ANGELINA PIKULIC
utterances.text: Well, yes, I did hear but we didn't dare go out. I did not dare go out.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What kind of weapons did you hear firing out there?

utterances.speaker: ANGELINA PIKULIC
utterances.text: I don't know. Something sort of stronger. Some kind of strong shooting, strong.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Stronger than a rifle?

utterances.speaker: ANGELINA PIKULIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Why did they arrest you?

utterances.speaker: ANGELINA PIKULIC
utterances.text: Because I stayed in Pofalici, because there was this big attack. They attacked all of Pofalici from the tobacco factory and from the side of Velesici, Pofalici, Buca Potok, and Um. Do you know where the relay is up there? That's where it started.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Who attacked and when did this happen?

utterances.speaker: ANGELINA PIKULIC
utterances.text: The 16th of May, May.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Who attacked?

utterances.speaker: ANGELINA PIKULIC
utterances.text: Well, this army, Alija's army. I mean, I could not recognise them. They weren't our people. I mean -- and there were some people who were speaking some kind of foreign language. I couldn't understand who they were and what they were and ...

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Were there any Serb soldiers in Pofalici?

utterances.speaker: ANGELINA PIKULIC
utterances.text: No. It was only Serb people from the city of Sarajevo, Cengic Villa, Pofalici, Marin Dvor, wherever Serbs were, they were fleeing through Zuc. They were escaping close to my house it was -- I mean, they were running in their slippers and they just had their little handbags.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You didn't manage to --

utterances.speaker: ANGELINA PIKULIC
utterances.text: My husband's relative and another lady relative and then there was this other woman who was a Muslim, a relative also, who was married to his son, and she stayed in my house. And then when they barged in and then she said, "Don't you go out, I will go out." And she walked out with her 2-month-old baby like this and she said, "What do you want from me?" We were in my basement in my house. There were 15 of us in my house.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Who were these 15 people who sought shelter there; right?

utterances.speaker: ANGELINA PIKULIC
utterances.text: Well, these people from Velesici who fled to my house. They're all from Velesici. They fled to my house. I just know my brother-in-law and that daughter-in-law of his and then their neighbours, I mean, they were all in my house.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Iodice.

utterances.speaker: MS. IODICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm afraid we're moving back to a topic that was excluded by the order of the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Excellency, I would like to establish whether this was a civilian settlement and whether there was a military presence there and whether there were any military installations there, military facilities, whether the witness could see something or hear something. We've heard about Velesici and now we're going to hear about Pofalici.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I don't understand the last sentence of your statement.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We heard that in Velesici there was a military presence and that there were heavy calibres firing from Velesici. Now I'd like to ask what was in Pofalici near her house. Obviously now we heard that she was saved by a Muslim lady who went out with her child and prevented them --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not hear what the witness said now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Without leading the witness, please put the question to the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you see some army in Pofalici around your house?

utterances.speaker: ANGELINA PIKULIC
utterances.text: Well, yes, I did. That time when they attacked they were all around the house and up there, and then my husband when this first attack took place, he escaped to the garage, and I stayed in the house with the relatives that I told you about just now. And then a soldier came to me and said, "You come with me." And I went along, above my house. There was this meadow up there, and he said, "Do you know these people who were killed there?" One man had his arm cut off and he said, "Gina, help me, save me." I couldn't even look and I felt sick and I turned my face away from him and went to the house. Do you want me to tell you who all the people were who got killed there?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: For the time being we're not going to deal with that, but it's a good thing that you told us that. Tell me, were there also some weapons, artillery pieces, or armoured vehicles there? What kind of military things could you see around your house?

utterances.speaker: ANGELINA PIKULIC
utterances.text: Around my house I saw them walking towards houses with rifles, and they were torching only Serb houses in Pofalici.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. What was in your garage?

utterances.speaker: ANGELINA PIKULIC
utterances.text: The police was in my garage.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What police was that?

utterances.speaker: ANGELINA PIKULIC
utterances.text: Alija's police.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Was there any shooting coming from the garage?

utterances.speaker: ANGELINA PIKULIC
utterances.text: Well, they opened fire and they wouldn't let me go out, and I was practically a hostage in my own home. I didn't dare go out.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you have a vacation home?

utterances.speaker: ANGELINA PIKULIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did. It was beyond Hum where you could go. There was this street going to Kobilja Glava, that's where I had the vacation home. I headed there with a friend of mine and another old woman who also wanted to see her own weekend or vacation home. And when we set off there we saw a head on a pike, and there was no body. We took a plastic bag and buried that head near Jovo Jovic's at Tresnija.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you see any military things, any vehicles or weapons, near your vacation home?

utterances.speaker: ANGELINA PIKULIC
utterances.text: Well, I did see some weapons, but I don't know whose it was. I just saw weapons a bit beyond my vacation home. It was near Hum.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. What did it look like?

utterances.speaker: ANGELINA PIKULIC
utterances.text: Well, it was amazing. I mean, it was weird so we returned right away, this woman, this lady, she helped me, she was a Catholic. And she said to me, "Come on, let's keep on moving, let's see Boza's house too." Her house, Boza's house had been torched, so was mine, and then we went back. When I came home -- when we arrived home we entered -- we went inside. There was an elderly woman with us, 93 years old, Pava Kadic, and all these people who were there, they were elderly. There were 13 elderly people in my home and I was the 14th. They -- they had brought them from this juvenile detention facility in Pofalici.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What was there at this juvenile facility?

utterances.speaker: ANGELINA PIKULIC
utterances.text: Well, it was a juvenile detention facility for young people, but all these elderly people they were detained there, all these people who were in my home had been detained there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, there was also a youth centre in Pofalici, wasn't there?

utterances.speaker: ANGELINA PIKULIC
utterances.text: Well, yes. Where IFOR was, some 10 metres away from my home, they were there. They distributed food. One day I got some food, but the following day I didn't. And they told me when I headed there for the second time with a pan, a pot, to get some food, they said to me, "No, you cannot get anything, you are not entitled to it." So I went back home. We had nothing to eat. We just struggled to survive. I had some wheat, or rather, some cattle fodder that I tried to use to bake bread, and that's what we ate.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now in lines 5 and 6 this was not my question. In English it sounds as a leading question, whereas my question was an open-ended question. Now, did you see any high officials from Bosnia and Herzegovina in your area?

utterances.speaker: ANGELINA PIKULIC
utterances.text: Yes, I saw Alija outside my door and he just said to his army, "Do not mention how many people you've killed."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Which Alija are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: ANGELINA PIKULIC
utterances.text: Well, Alija Izetbegovic, he was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I see that this Catholic woman helped you?

utterances.speaker: ANGELINA PIKULIC
utterances.text: She was the one who helped me most.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Please pause before you start answering. Now, were there also such cases, such instances, where the Muslims would help, that you lived together well and you helped each other out?

utterances.speaker: ANGELINA PIKULIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's true. There were Muslims that I knew who helped me. That's the truth. I cannot not say that, not confirm that. They helped me. They brought some sugar and oil. Ramiz and his son defended us. Now, he was killed and when he saw who had killed my son he came from my back garden and he was calling me, "Gina, Gina," although my real name is Angelina, he said, "Gina, Gina, my son was not killed by Chetniks, but rather by Ustashas." This was Ramiz.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, what was the majority population in Pofalici?

utterances.speaker: ANGELINA PIKULIC
utterances.text: Serb.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you understand the fact that Ramiz's son was killed, that he was killed because he helped Serbs?

utterances.speaker: ANGELINA PIKULIC
utterances.text: Well, yes, that's what his father said. That's not what I said. He came and said that.

utterances.speaker: MS. IODICE
utterances.text: Objection. We're again getting away from the topics discussed in the statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Let the evidence flow for some time. I take it that you are coming to an end, Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Excellency. Just one last question. Could we now have P9573, page 82 in e-court -- my apologies 793 -- 973, P973, not 5. P, Prosecution exhibit, yes. Could we see page 82, please. Page 82 of this document, not the e-court page. In other words, three pages further. Thank you. This is good.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mrs. Pikulic, I will read out to you now what an expert said here before this Court while testifying and then I will put a question to you. I will read this in English, unfortunately, but you will get the interpretation. Towards the top of the page, line 1. [In English] "Karadzic wrote in an open letter to UN Secretary-General Boutros Boutros-Ghali 'between 40.000 to 50.000 Serbs are held as ethnic hostages and the constant daily attacks on Serbian municipalities, Ilidza, Lukavica, Ilijas, Vogosca take place.'" [Interpretation] Did you hear this interpreted that I read, that in Sarajevo there were 40.000 to 50.000 Serbs who were ethnic hostages, which meant that they were not allowed to leave their homes or move around freely and cross over to the Serb territory, and is that true as far as you know?

utterances.speaker: MS. IODICE
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, how is she in a position to comment upon an expert report? That's already in our evidence. I don't see the point of putting that question to this witness, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, Mr. President, I think the point is that in paragraph 14 of the indictment under (c)(i) in particular, Dr. Karadzic is charged with disseminating propaganda to -- false propaganda intended to engender fear and hatred of Bosnian Muslims or Croats by Bosnian Serbs, including that the Serbs were in danger of oppression including genocide, among other things. So Mr. Donia testified that among the propaganda that Dr. Karadzic was promulgating was the fact that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Madam Pikulic, do you understand English?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could you kindly -- could you kindly put down your headphones for some time. Thank you. Yes, Mr. Robinson, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. So Dr. Donia testified that among the propaganda that was made by Dr. Karadzic was that Serbs were being held as ethnic hostages in Sarajevo. And so Dr. Karadzic would like to ask this witness who was in Sarajevo at the time whether or not what he said was true or whether he was merely stating false propaganda.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Ms. Iodice, I remember you were on your feet. Would you like to respond?

utterances.speaker: MS. IODICE
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. First of all, this is again a topic that the Trial Chamber excluded already; and second, I don't see how this witness can confirm or deny such a broad statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Any specific response to Mr. Robinson's point?

utterances.speaker: MS. IODICE
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, that this -- there's no notice that this witness would testify on this issue and the issues that this witness is supposed to testify have been identified by the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So is it your point that the accused is not entitled to put other relevant questions except for what is contained in her previous statement, Ms. Iodice?

utterances.speaker: MS. IODICE
utterances.text: That was my understanding from the Trial Chamber's order, that he was entitled to put questions regarding military targets in Pofalici and Velesici.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. President, two things. Number one, we did give notice to the Prosecution yesterday. I sent them an e-mail telling them that we would be using the specific exhibit 973, so they had notice of it. And secondly --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: 973 is a very voluminous --

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: -- document.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes it is. And secondly, we understood that once you've converted this witness into a viva voce witness there was limitations of what was excluded but not necessarily what topics were to be included in her testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The Chamber will allow the question. Please continue, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mrs. Pikulic, a few moments ago in one of your answers you said that you were not allowed to leave your home and that you were a hostage in our own house. Now I've just read out to you that I wrote to the general secretary of the UN that there were 40.000 to 50.000 Serbs in Sarajevo who were held hostage who were not free. Now, according to what you know, were there and how many of them any Serbs in Sarajevo and were they free to move around or leave Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: ANGELINA PIKULIC
utterances.text: Well, I first asked them to allow me to leave with my husband because my husband had been transferred to Kasindol where the hospital was. So I asked them to let me go with him but they wouldn't let me, and I remained with these old people and in 1993 he died.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you know anything else about any other Serbs?

utterances.speaker: ANGELINA PIKULIC
utterances.text: Well, there were our Serbs who weren't allowed to -- they couldn't leave or go out anywhere unless they allowed them. When they said -- I wasn't even allowed to go fetch some water until they said you can go and fetch water.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, what I said here, these things that I said, was that propaganda? Were those lies? Or rather, can you tell me what kind of position were they in and whether what I was saying was an exaggeration?

utterances.speaker: ANGELINA PIKULIC
utterances.text: No, no --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, that's not a proper question for this witness.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Were you allowed to attend the funeral?

utterances.speaker: ANGELINA PIKULIC
utterances.text: No. I begged them to let me go. I didn't even know the date when he died. I was just informed. I received a notice from the Red Cross. They said, "Your husband had died." They wouldn't let me go to Saravica [phoen]. This was at Grbavica. My husband was at his sister's at Grbavica. So he was buried by -- only in the presence of my sister and her sister and --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness repeat the last part of her answer, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Ms. Pikulic, could you repeated your last part of your answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What happened? Well, I said what I knew, just what I said a moment ago, that I wasn't allowed to attend my husband's funeral. The Red Cross came. They informed me that my husband had passed away. They didn't let me go. His sister buried him there and it was only in 1994, on the 3rd of July, that I was able to get out.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. But you said something about Grbavica, that someone had been killed by a sniper?

utterances.speaker: ANGELINA PIKULIC
utterances.text: Yes, this was my brother-in-law, my sister's husband. He was killed by a sniper.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Whose sniper? Was that ever determined?

utterances.speaker: ANGELINA PIKULIC
utterances.text: Well, they said it wasn't from the Serb side. It was from Alija's side. If you know Grbavica, the main road leading to Grbavica, this is where he was crossing going to the market and that's where he was hit by a sniper.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Was he a soldier or a civilian?

utterances.speaker: ANGELINA PIKULIC
utterances.text: He was a civilian. He was a retiree.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mrs. Pikulic. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: ANGELINA PIKULIC
utterances.text: Never mind. Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Iodice.

utterances.speaker: MS. IODICE
utterances.text: Mrs. Pikulic?

utterances.speaker: ANGELINA PIKULIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. IODICE
utterances.text: You don't have any military education; correct?

utterances.speaker: ANGELINA PIKULIC
utterances.text: No, I don't. No, none of that.

utterances.speaker: MS. IODICE
utterances.text: And when you -- you said today that you couldn't leave your house in Pofalici; correct?

utterances.speaker: ANGELINA PIKULIC
utterances.text: Yes, I could not leave. I wasn't allowed to. They didn't let me.

utterances.speaker: MS. IODICE
utterances.text: And you -- while you were in your house in Pofalici you went to the Presidency building; correct?

utterances.speaker: ANGELINA PIKULIC
utterances.text: Yes, I went to the Presidency building because that's where I used to work. I thought I will find my colleagues there and I went looking for food. We didn't have any food.

utterances.speaker: MS. IODICE
utterances.text: And so you were allowed to go to the Presidency building?

utterances.speaker: ANGELINA PIKULIC
utterances.text: Well, yes. I asked them to let me go and they said, "Why do you want to go there?" And I said, "Well, I want to go to look for some food. I know those people because I used to work for them."

utterances.speaker: MS. IODICE
utterances.text: And in the Presidency building you saw -- you say you saw two men and you didn't recognise any of them; right?

utterances.speaker: ANGELINA PIKULIC
utterances.text: No, I didn't. How could I? When I saw someone screaming there and then this guy was opening the door and then I saw this one who was covered and the other one was naked. When I saw that, I just fled and I started running towards the mosque and the hospital towards my house.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It didn't make it into the transcript: When I saw that suffering.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, yes, I felt sick.

utterances.speaker: MS. IODICE
utterances.text: So you don't know what their ethnicity was or what had happened to them; correct?

utterances.speaker: ANGELINA PIKULIC
utterances.text: No. No, I didn't. I didn't know anything. I just saw that and I fled that place. I ran towards the mosque and this is the way to my home in the direction of the military hospital. So I walked all the way to Pofalici because there was no transportation. I had a lot of friends. Everyone knew me. I can't really say anything about who is what. There were good people and there were also others who were God forbid.

utterances.speaker: MS. IODICE
utterances.text: Thank you. And you said today that while you were in Pofalici you also went to see your house at -- your weekend house at Hum, correct, in Kobilja Glava; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ANGELINA PIKULIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. IODICE
utterances.text: Was Pofalici a residential area?

utterances.speaker: ANGELINA PIKULIC
utterances.text: Pofalici? What do you mean was it ...?

utterances.speaker: MS. IODICE
utterances.text: There were houses. People lived there; correct? There were many houses?

utterances.speaker: ANGELINA PIKULIC
utterances.text: Well, these were all houses where people lived, our Serb people and Muslim people and Catholic people, that's what it was. There were Serbs and Catholics and Muslims, Bosniaks. But the majority in Pofalici were Serbian.

utterances.speaker: MS. IODICE
utterances.text: And Velesici was also a residential area - right? - with many apartment buildings and houses; correct?

utterances.speaker: ANGELINA PIKULIC
utterances.text: Well, there too there were Serbs --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not hear the rest.

utterances.speaker: MS. IODICE
utterances.text: Yes, but my question was simply whether there were apartment buildings and houses, only about whether it's a residential area. Yes or no?

utterances.speaker: ANGELINA PIKULIC
utterances.text: In Velesici there were buildings, there were houses, there were Serb people, Catholic people, Bosniaks, Muslims. It was all mixed. There were people of all faiths.

utterances.speaker: MS. IODICE
utterances.text: Thank you. And when you say that during your time in Velesici that was about ten days that you spent there, you heard explosion, noises. You didn't see what was happening; correct? You just heard the noises?

utterances.speaker: ANGELINA PIKULIC
utterances.text: I only heard the noises and firing. We weren't -- they didn't let us leave our houses where we were.

utterances.speaker: MS. IODICE
utterances.text: If you can bear with me for a second, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. IODICE
utterances.text: Mrs. Pikulic in -- and this is page 10, line 20 of the transcript today, you said that you saw Alija Izetbegovic outside your house and he mentioned --

utterances.speaker: ANGELINA PIKULIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did. I saw Alija right in front of my house and he said, "Don't say how many you've killed." He said that at a place that was no more than 2 metres away from my house.

utterances.speaker: MS. IODICE
utterances.text: And that's something that you would have remembered, right? It's something very important that you could not forget; right?

utterances.speaker: ANGELINA PIKULIC
utterances.text: I'll never forget that, never. It's in my head. I will always remember that.

utterances.speaker: MS. IODICE
utterances.text: Now if we can call up 1D6037. You gave a statement in October 1995 and you agree with me that your recollection of the events at that time was much better than it is today; right?

utterances.speaker: ANGELINA PIKULIC
utterances.text: I gave a statement in 1995.

utterances.speaker: MS. IODICE
utterances.text: And that's the statement that you can see in front of you right now. You should be able to see it?

utterances.speaker: ANGELINA PIKULIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. IODICE
utterances.text: In 1995 your memory of the events was fresher and was much better than it is today; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ANGELINA PIKULIC
utterances.text: Well, yes. Everything I've said I'm saying today as well. What I said in 1995 is what I'm saying today. I am saying what it was that I saw. I cannot talk at all about what I have not seen.

utterances.speaker: MS. IODICE
utterances.text: Right. But in this statement you did not mention this very important detail of Alija Izetbegovic telling to someone not to mention how many people they've killed, nowhere in this statement can we find any mention of that detail, that you said you will never forget.

utterances.speaker: ANGELINA PIKULIC
utterances.text: I did see Mr. Izetbegovic in front of my door and that's what he said. I'll never forget that. That will remain in my head for as long as I live.

utterances.speaker: MS. IODICE
utterances.text: Mrs. Pikulic, I understand that you're now saying that you saw Mr. Izetbegovic, but you do understand that you never mentioned this detail before? This very important detail, you never mentioned it to anyone before - right? - when you were interviewed about the crimes; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ANGELINA PIKULIC
utterances.text: Yes, I said that earlier on too.

utterances.speaker: MS. IODICE
utterances.text: And in the two statements that you've given up to today, both the 1995 statement and the statement that you gave to the Defence and you signed, you did not mention this?

utterances.speaker: ANGELINA PIKULIC
utterances.text: I mentioned that. Alija Izetbegovic was in front of my house and I will say that whenever. That's the same statement that I made in 1995. There's that statement of mine there. Read it. See what I said there.

utterances.speaker: MS. IODICE
utterances.text: I've read it and there's no mention, but I'll leave it at that.

utterances.speaker: MS. IODICE
utterances.text: I have no further questions, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Robinson, you would agree that there is no mention of Izetbegovic in this statement?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. But I think perhaps the statement --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There is.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: The statement --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: We could all look at the statement, it should be admitted, I think, and then everybody can see it for themselves.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I don't see a point of admitting this statement for that purpose. Yes, Mr. Karadzic -- I take it, Ms. Iodice, you're not tendering that statement, are you?

utterances.speaker: MS. IODICE
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, I'm not tendering the statement, but I think we can agree with the Defence that there's no mention in that statement and in the Defence statement that they prepared.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That was my understanding. Mr. Karadzic, do you have any re-examination?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just two questions, Your Excellency.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mrs. Pikulic, when did you go to the Presidency -- or rather, when you went, was it necessary to ask for permission?

utterances.speaker: ANGELINA PIKULIC
utterances.text: It wasn't because there was this doorman who worked there and he recognised me. He said, "What are you doing here?" And I said, "I came to get some food." And he said, "You wait here by the reception desk," and the reception desk is nearby. And then there was this other room that was an office, and that's where women typed on typewriters and that's where it was. And then when I saw this man walking out -- I mean, I heard this screaming and I looked at all of that and --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. However, for you to go from your house to the Presidency, could you freely do that or did you need to get permission for that?

utterances.speaker: ANGELINA PIKULIC
utterances.text: The policeman who was in front of my door in my garage, he's the one who had to allow me to do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: ANGELINA PIKULIC
utterances.text: They know that I worked there in that company, so they let me go.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. After you gave this statement in 1996, did you ever read it again? I mean, have you read it recently?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: The first statement you gave in 1995 or 1996.

utterances.speaker: ANGELINA PIKULIC
utterances.text: It was in 1995. I got out in 1994 and I gave the statement in 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: After that, have you ever read it?

utterances.speaker: ANGELINA PIKULIC
utterances.text: What? You mean my statement? Yes. I have this newspaper at home, I have all of it, I should have brought that along, I really should have, and you would have seen that that's exactly the way it was. Well, anyway, I can send it to you. I can send you those newspapers and you see for yourself.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did they ask you anything about Alija Izetbegovic in 1995?

utterances.speaker: ANGELINA PIKULIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. They asked me from the very beginning, just as I told you at -- like you're asking me now, but then you skipped certain things. I mean, I don't understand any of this. I just understand how it is that I'm supposed to talk from the very beginning. From 1992 until -- until the 16th of May -- I mean, I can tell you all of that straight-out of my head and you've heard some of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam. It is our responsibility because we had to limit our questions.

utterances.speaker: ANGELINA PIKULIC
utterances.text: Ah, all right. But if you wish I can send you those newspapers. I have all of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Just one question. Did you mention Izetbegovic in the newspapers?

utterances.speaker: ANGELINA PIKULIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I did. And, if necessary, I'll send those newspapers to the Court.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There you go, it is in the newspapers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, thank you, Mrs. Pikulic. That concludes your evidence at the Tribunal. On behalf of this Chamber I would like to thank you for your coming to The Hague to give us. Now you are free to go.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I wish you all the very best too, and thank you for receiving me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could the Chamber move into private session briefly.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Back in open session.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Your Honours. Just a moment of brief indulgence. Sorry, I'm over here because I don't have direct eye contact with Your Honours otherwise. I'll be leading the next witness. I wonder if we could just have about three minutes to switch places; I'll do it as fast as I can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you for the indulgence, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So let me going back to the previous issue since Ms. Iodice is here. If the Defence does not agree that the previous witness mentioned in her previous statement that Alija Izetbegovic was mentioned in the statement, probably we need to admit that statement for that purpose only. But --

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. President, we agree that it's not in the statement. So we would like to have -- we prefer to have the statement admitted, obviously, but we're not going to dispute that it's not there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I think that suffices. Thank you. Would the witness take the solemn declaration, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Please make yourself comfortable. Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Ms. Pandurevic.

utterances.speaker: RADOJKA PANDUREVIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Right from the start I have to ask you to pause between questions and answers, as we don't want to wear out our interpreters and we want to have everything in the record, in the transcript. Could we please both have this in mind.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could I have 1D6703 in e-court. Your Excellencies, does this mean that you will accept the news article referred to by the witness if you found it to be relevant?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Let's deal with it when it arises, when it's necessary. Let's move on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Ms. Pandurevic, did you provide a statement to the Defence team and do you see it before you on the screen now?

utterances.speaker: RADOJKA PANDUREVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did, and I accept it in full as it stands.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: We have it here in English, but have you read it in the Serbian language and does it accurately reflect what you wanted to say?

utterances.speaker: RADOJKA PANDUREVIC
utterances.text: I read the statement, but it doesn't reflect accurately everything I said, as I can see that some portions are marked which were unacceptable and redacted. Those paragraphs have to do with my stay in the Silos camp, which in turn would mean that I cannot convey the suffering I had undergone in the Silos camp.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: As for the rest, the part of the statement that was not redacted, is it true?

utterances.speaker: RADOJKA PANDUREVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you sign it?

utterances.speaker: RADOJKA PANDUREVIC
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: If I were to ask you today the same questions concerning the unredacted portion, would your answers be the same in essence?

utterances.speaker: RADOJKA PANDUREVIC
utterances.text: They would.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I seek to tender the 65 ter package -- sorry, the 92 ter package with five associated exhibits?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. President, we are offering only the first five associated exhibits on our Rule 92 ter listing because the others are covered by paragraphs which are redacted. And for these five we would also ask for permission to add them to our 65 ter list because they were not loaded into e-court at the time of the 65 ter list was due.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The last two of those five items were not translated, are they?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: If they're not in e-court with translations then they haven't been translated, so we would withdraw them at this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I'm referring to 1D13010 and 1D13011.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Which are dealt with in para 56. If you'd like to deal with -- I would like the accused to deal with the witness live so that we can follow what it is about at least, but you said you are minded to withdraw that document?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: If you give me a moment to discuss with Dr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: We're going to check and see if we can release the translations, see what the problem is. But in the meantime perhaps he can read the summary and we'll try to have that information after the summary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Any objections, Ms. Edgerton?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: First we will admit the redacted version of Rule 92 ter statement.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. 65 ter 1D6703 will be Exhibit D2490.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And then we'll admit the first three associated exhibits.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. 65 ter number 1D3007 will be Exhibit D2491, 65 ter number 1D3008 will be Exhibit D2492, and 65 ter number 1D3009 will be Exhibit D2493.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, please continue, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I will read out a summary concerning the unredacted part of the witness's statement by Ms. Pandurevic in the English language. [In English] Radojka Pandurevic was a member of the SDS Hadzici Municipal Board and president of the SDS local board in Rastelica. After the multi-party election in 1990 she was elected deputy in the Hadzici Municipal Assembly. She regularly attended the sessions of the Hadzici SDS Municipal Board, but they never received orders from the SDS centre. At the meetings they discussed the problems that were present and were thinking about how to rescue their own families and property. The head of the Hadzici SJB Fadil Covic, the Muslim, started a mass mobilisation of the reserve police forces, mainly Muslims, without the commander's knowledge. Commander was a Serb. At the first Assembly meeting after these events, the Serbs asked to have the matter put on the agenda in order to contest the mobilisation only of Muslims. However, the Muslims did not want to discuss this, and the Serbian deputies left the Assembly. After the Muslim attack and occupation of Bradina on 26th of May, 1992, and Bradina was a Serbian village, Muslims started arresting Serbs in Rastelica and ordering them to surrender their weapons. Radojka Pandurevic and her family felt unsafe and left to Gornja Rastelica the same day, 28th of May, 1992. Upon her arrival she was taken to meet with Tufo Refik, a Muslim gentleman to give him information about weapons. After this, she and her daughter were taken to the woods and the Muslims threatened the locals hiding there to surrender. They were then taken to the social centre and the Silos in Tarcin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, does that not cover the redacted part?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's but one sentence, Your Excellency, to simply see what she had gone through rather than going into what her treatment was at the camp.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No, it's -- there's no point if it is not in the evidence. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: On 26th of January, 1996, after almost four years of detention, she was taken out from the Silos camp by the members of the international police and taken to her mother's.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Um, Your Honour, that information was also redacted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please bear in mind that your summary which you read out is not a part of evidence at all. So bear that in mind.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Excellencies, I wanted to ask Madam about things that are in the indictment, and for that I need to know and demonstrate where she was and how she knew about that, let alone the fact that I am of the opinion that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: If it is necessary, Mr. Karadzic and it is not covered by the remainder of her statement, i.e., that the part of the statement which is not redacted, then you need -- you should put that question to the witness live.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I will correct that immediately.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Ms. Pandurevic, before 1990 you were not involved in politics, were you?

utterances.speaker: RADOJKA PANDUREVIC
utterances.text: I was not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What was the reason for you entering politics?

utterances.speaker: RADOJKA PANDUREVIC
utterances.text: As you well know, in early 1990 the Muslim party, SDA, was established. Immediately following their establishment, the HDZ was established with its seat in Tarcin. They had a church there and there were many Croats living there. The last party to be established was the Serb Democratic Party which was in September 1990. After the party was established, a pre-electoral campaign took off and thus lists were drafted for the Municipal Assembly of Hadzici municipality. As the deputies lists were being created for the Hadzici Municipal Assembly, my colleagues, Muslims, started driving around the village in their vehicles, sporting the SDA flag. On the Serb weekend homes they painted graffiti with the SDA signs and the crescent moon. When my husband and I became married, we came to Rastica, to my father-in-law's property, and we were not well received by our neighbours, as we were both employed and were an educated couple. My father-in-law's family suffered a lot during World War II and he's the only one who survived it because he happened not to be at home. It happened between the 4th and 5th of April, 1945. Only another sister of his survived. She was wounded and taken by Germans to Mostar. He found her two years later. Because of all these events, there was concern that one morning my house will also be painted with SDA signs. That's why I went to Hadzici to the seat of the SDS. Although I had only been a sympathiser up until then, I asked to become a member and to be placed on a list of deputies to be elected to the Hadzici Municipal Assembly. I wanted to be among the first people on the list so that I would make sure I became a deputy in order to be part of the executive branch. Many of my neighbours who ran for deputies and were on the SDA list were well-known criminals with police files. The very idea that they would participate in the work of the executive branch thus deciding on the quality of my life and the life of my fellow citizens in the municipality and to make important decisions made me to take this action. I wanted to sit alongside those people in the Municipal Assembly in order to hear what they had to say so that I would be able to react at any given point in time. That was the reason why I joined the SDS.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Your Honours, if I may. Your Honours, the Prosecution has had no notice of this evidence nor in your ruling yesterday was Dr. Karadzic or was there any indication, as I read the ruling, that Dr. Karadzic would be allowed to lead evidence viva voce on matters relevant to the indictment otherwise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, you are well aware of the Court's ruling and I believe that you can monitor your and control your examination-in-chief. Do you follow, Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do, Your Honour, but I also understand the witness who suffered and wanted to discuss that. I was only interested in her reasons for joining politics, since she was an educated person.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Well, Dr. Karadzic, everybody understands that where an individual has suffered egregiously that at some point they like to have a hearing as to that. But the reality of the position in which we find ourselves is this is not the right forum for that and accordingly the limitations have been put on. This is not out of a lack of sympathy for the witness; it's to expedite the proceeding.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In the briefest possible terms, can you tell us what was the basis for your arrest?

utterances.speaker: RADOJKA PANDUREVIC
utterances.text: The basis for my arrest was my work in the parliament -- or actually in the Municipal Assembly in Hadzici, since I was an SDS deputy and because I was a Serb.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Were there other women who were arrested and what was their ethnicity? Also, why were they arrested?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I'm sorry --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, again --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: -- Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Again, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you ever see me in Hadzici? Did I come to Hadzici while you were there?

utterances.speaker: RADOJKA PANDUREVIC
utterances.text: No, I never saw you in Hadzici. I only saw you once in passing during the founding Assembly and today I see you for the second time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: The founding Assembly where?

utterances.speaker: RADOJKA PANDUREVIC
utterances.text: In Sarajevo, in Skenderija.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: When?

utterances.speaker: RADOJKA PANDUREVIC
utterances.text: The 12th of July, 1990.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have 1D6702. Your Excellencies, I was told that we have been provided with the translations of these two documents, they have been sent by e-mail. By your leave perhaps they can be placed in e-court. First we would need the technician to upload it into e-court, as my case manager does not have direct access.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Ms. Pandurevic, what is this? What is the letter or the note on the screen?

utterances.speaker: RADOJKA PANDUREVIC
utterances.text: It is a letter by Ms. Elisabeth Rehn who answered my daughter, Aleksandra. She had met with her in early January 1996. My daughter, Aleksandra, asked her to intervene with the BH authorities, with Alija Izetbegovic specifically, to have the remaining 43 Serbs released who were kept in the Silos camp. She promised she would try to do so; however, I happened to have been released before Ms. Rehn arrived in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Which parts of Hadzici municipality was -- were controlled by the Serb side and which parts were controlled by the Muslim side and what was the proportion in terms of size?

utterances.speaker: RADOJKA PANDUREVIC
utterances.text: The Serb side controlled part of Hadzici municipality between Ilidza and the quarry in Hadzici. From that point and Dazaric [phoen] and Tarcin, all of the surrounding villages were controlled by the Muslim side.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did the Serbs control some Muslim settlements or, to put it in these terms, did the armies control their respective territories?

utterances.speaker: RADOJKA PANDUREVIC
utterances.text: The Muslims predominantly controlled the territory inhabited by Muslims, and the Serbs controlled the centre of Hadzici and the nearby villages which were populated by Serbs for the most part.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: How about the -- those two untranslated documents? Yes, Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, they're received and sent by e-mail but not uploaded in e-court yet. So if you -- I'll leave it to Dr. Karadzic. My recommendation has been not to pursue it and take our time with that, but he may feel differently.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, I get -- I'll turn to you, Ms. Edgerton. 1D13010 and 11 which are a part of the associated exhibits without English translation.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I've been looking at those, Your Honours, and frankly I think the exhibits -- or potential exhibits actually speak for themselves and I don't quite find them to be what the witness alleges them to be, so I would be uncomfortable dealing with them in an untranslated manner.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No, you didn't receive English translation?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Oh, no.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We have received it by e-mail but our ...

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I've just been told, Your Honours -- oh, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I think you were excluded in the recipients. It must be received -- must have been received by other members of the OTP.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Well, if I was to look at my e-mail, but I don't watch it while I'm trying to listen to the witness, I might have seen them eventually from Mr. Reid. If you want them dealt with now, I'm happy to take a couple of minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yeah, we'll cover that at the end of the evidence of this witness. So you don't have any further questions for the witness?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour. Should we also tender Ms. Elisabeth Rehn's letter since she was a prominent figure? She tried to intervene after the war to have those people released.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well, we'll admit it. Yes, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Well, given that Your Honour's have already ruled, I'd still like to make the comment that I find the content of this letter and the witness's comments thereon to be effectively almost a backdoor way of getting around Your Honour's earlier ruling with respect to the redactions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. I thought you were not objecting to it. I'll consult my colleagues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I was too quick and then I -- the Chamber will not receive it based upon the ruling we gave previously. Given the time, we'll continue after the break, but Ms. -- Mrs. Pandurevic, as you have noted, your evidence in chief was admitted in most part by way of written evidence in lieu of your oral testimony. You will now be cross-examined by the Prosecution after the break.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Why cannot the addition, my oral addition, to the statement be admitted as well?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, it is already transcribed. It is in the evidence. We'll have a break for an hour and resume at 1.30. --- Luncheon recess taken at 12.29 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Have the parties resolved the issue with respect to those two associated exhibits? Otherwise, I would like you -- Mr. Karadzic to deal with viva voce with the witness if he's minded to tender those two documents. Yes, Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. I don't know what the Prosecutor's position is, but they did make it into e-court now so that we do have English translations in e-court and we'll be guided by whether the Prosecution will accept that or whether they wish to hear viva voce testimony about it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The Chamber was unable to discern whether it constituted inseparable and indispensable part of the statement because we couldn't read it. But for the sake of time I'll turn to Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Um, now having read the documents, I am satisfied that the documents do speak for themselves, and for that reason I won't object to their admission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Given the circumstances, we'll admit those two documents into evidence and give the numbers.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. 65 ter number 13010 will be Exhibit D2494 and 65 ter number 13011 will be Exhibit D2495.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Hello, Mrs. Pandurevic.

utterances.speaker: RADOJKA PANDUREVIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Madam Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. So I take it you can hear me in a language you understand?

utterances.speaker: RADOJKA PANDUREVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Just one question of Your Honours before I go any further. I haven't received any guidance from Your Honours on the issue of time that I have available. Just for my own sake and planning, I wonder if I could hear your guidance?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Were you not informed of the amount of time? How long would you need?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: 45 minutes or less.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I could -- I take it you could finish it in half an hour.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Mrs. Pandurevic, I'd like to ask you some questions based on the statement that you gave, but just before I do that I wonder if you could confirm for us that you were present at the constitutive meeting of the Assembly of the Serbian Municipality of Hadzici on 11 April 1992?

utterances.speaker: RADOJKA PANDUREVIC
utterances.text: No, I was not present because that Assembly was held in the afternoon hours and there were already concerns about me having to travel because I live some 10 kilometres away from the Hadzici municipality. And for security reasons, because every day I would have to go through four check-points to get to Hadzici, I did not dare, being a woman, to go so late in such late afternoon to attend the Constituent Assembly, but I do know what was happening there, which organs were elected, and who was elected.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Maybe on that point we could have a look at a document. It's P2297. It's the minutes of the meeting of that Assembly. And if -- just take a few minutes and look at this because it's handwritten. And they're dated on 11 April 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And if we could go over to English page 3 and B/C/S page 4. And that page is a list of those present at the Assembly of the Serbian People of Hadzici.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, do you see your name in the column that's in -- the page that's in your language on the left-hand column at number 18, your name and your signature?

utterances.speaker: RADOJKA PANDUREVIC
utterances.text: Yes, my printed first and last name, that's a list of Assemblymen but I don't see that I've signed it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Let's collapse the English page and --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know about that because I know for certain that I wasn't present.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Do you see number 18? We can only see the 8.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do, I see it. I see 8 and I see my first and last name, but I was not present at this constitutive Assembly. Perhaps I did affix my signature later on for some other reasons because they were necessary, but I did not attend, I know for sure, because it was held in the afternoon. But yes, this is my signature.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So you having recognised your signature then, we can move on. Just another question that perhaps you can confirm to me. Can you confirm that you were captured on 28 May 1992? Just a yes or no as to the date would be fine?

utterances.speaker: RADOJKA PANDUREVIC
utterances.text: Yes, the 28th of May, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I just request about this first document where it says that this was the Constituent Assembly, because it may have been one of the assemblies because it didn't say there that this was a list of those present at the Constituent Assembly could we just see the first page, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: The source for my assertion that it was the Constituent Assembly comes from the evidence of Mr. Glavas before Your Honours and if I can -- I can either move on and give Your Honours the exhibit number for his written evidence later or I can take a couple of moments and give you that number now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I think it would suffice to provide that information outside the courtroom to the Defence. Let's move on.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So now in your statement at paragraph 63, referring to the formation of the Crisis Staff, are we meant to understand then that the Crisis Staff of the Serbian municipality of Hadzici had not been formed before 28 May 1992?

utterances.speaker: RADOJKA PANDUREVIC
utterances.text: When the Crisis Staff of the Serbian Municipality of Hadzici, I don't know, because I could not go to the Serb part of the Hadzici municipality after the 4th of May because the war had already broken out and it wasn't safe. So the 4th of May was the last day when I was actually in Hadzici.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Ah, so when you said in your statement that you -- that it hadn't been formed before the 28th of May, you actually meant to say you didn't know when it was formed; is that correct ?

utterances.speaker: RADOJKA PANDUREVIC
utterances.text: I don't know. No, I don't know when exactly it was established, but I assume that by the time I was arrested on the 28th of May it hadn't been established. And the 4th of May was the last day when I was in the -- on the territory of the municipality of Hadzici.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Let's have a look at D1084.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: It's a document dated 26th of May, 1992, signed by Ratko Radic. You know who Ratko Radic is, Mrs. Pandurevic?

utterances.speaker: RADOJKA PANDUREVIC
utterances.text: Ratko Radic was the president of the SDS and later on, after the 20th or the 28th - I'm not sure of the date -- because up until I was arrested Ratko Radic was not the president of the Municipal Assembly nor was he the president of the Crisis Staff, but I do know that he was the chairman of the Serbian Democratic Party. And I don't know. I didn't even know who the members of the Crisis Staff were because I had already been cut off from the headquarters, the municipality, the party, and so on. So I don't know these things. The communications did not exist.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So if I could just get you to have a look at this document which is signed by Ratko Radic as president of the Crisis Staff. And at the very top line of the document reads: "At a meeting of the Hadzici Serb Municipality Crisis Staff we pass the following decisions ..." And note that the document is dated 28th -- pardon me, 26th May, 1992. You would concede then that the -- on the basis of this document it looks as though the Crisis Staff was functioning by the date of your arrest?

utterances.speaker: RADOJKA PANDUREVIC
utterances.text: I don't know anything about that because there was no communication between me and the municipality of Hadzici or the party, so I wouldn't know anything about that.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: All right. Now, also in your statement at paragraph 61, and it's in regard to the activity of the SDS Municipal Board for Hadzici, you said: "I claim with full responsibility we never received any orders from the top, the SDS centre ..." And then you said Ratko Radic never told you about anything being an order from the SDS Main Board or President Karadzic and that you made all the decisions on your own. Now, do you mean by saying that to suggest that the SDS party structure was not hierarchical?

utterances.speaker: RADOJKA PANDUREVIC
utterances.text: Could you please just clarify a bit?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: When you say you got no orders from the top, do you mean to suggest that the SDS party structure was something other than hierarchical, that it didn't have a hierarchical structure?

utterances.speaker: RADOJKA PANDUREVIC
utterances.text: There was no need for any orders because at the time the party was busy with being established, the establishment of lists of candidates and Assemblymen, and busy organising the structure of government at the period. Ratko Radic did have communications. He contacted the main headquarters of the Serbian Democratic Party, but he never brought back with him any orders or anything of that sort. We dealt with our own problems in the Hadzici municipality because we had major problems from the very first days of the establishment of the municipality with the functioning of the organs, the political organs. So there was no need to get any orders. These were local issues that were dealt with.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So you're not disputing that the party had a hierarchical structure with Dr. Karadzic at the top?

utterances.speaker: RADOJKA PANDUREVIC
utterances.text: Well, as far as I know, the contacts did exist but this was not in any sense a situation where orders would be issued nor were there any obligations that someone would issue orders. Strictly speaking, absolutely not, and especially President Karadzic never issued any orders either written or signed or anything of that sort -- at least I never saw it.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Well, I'd like to go to another document. If you tell me you'd like to see it I'll have it called up for you. For the record, it's P961, the minutes of the -- pardon me, the stenograph of the Assembly of the Serbian People on 24 March, 1992, English page 22, paragraph 5, and B/C/S page 39, paragraph 2. I'm a bit confused about this assertion because on that day, 24 March, Dr. Karadzic told the delegates the following. He said: "We have a legal basis on the Law on Internal Affairs and we also have the insignia and at a desired moment, and this will be very soon, we can form whatever we want. There are reasons why this could happen in two or three days. Such are the forecasts but I can't tell you the reasons now. At that moment, all the Serbian municipalities, both the old ones and the newly established ones, would literally assume control of the entire territory of the municipality concerned." And further he says then: "At a given moment in the next three or four days there will be a single method used and you will be able to apply it in the municipalities you represent, including both things that must be done as well as how to do them, how to separate the police force, take the resources that belong to the Serbian people, and take command." So now, Mrs. Pandurevic, actually it looks like that, in fact, the very act that we talked about, the formation of the Assembly of Serbian people of Hadzici, a very significant act for the Serbian people there, wasn't an autonomous decision. That was a decision taken by the Serbian people according to a directive by Dr. Karadzic in the SDS. Wouldn't you agree?

utterances.speaker: RADOJKA PANDUREVIC
utterances.text: Could you please just clarify what date, on what May was it that Dr. Karadzic issued that order?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: This was what Dr. Karadzic said to delegates in the Assembly of Serbian People on 24 March 1992.

utterances.speaker: RADOJKA PANDUREVIC
utterances.text: The deputies of the Hadzici Municipal Assembly had already as of October 1992 departed from the Municipal Assembly of Hadzici and its work because of the reports we received on the work of the police because of their disagreement with the replacement of all the managers in schools, companies, and medical centres in Hadzici, especially so because the municipality was not really authorised to replace people in certain organisations because they were under the management of the town itself, not the municipality. And because we couldn't get that information from the reserve force, police force, and we could not get their -- the decision saying that there was an agreement on replacing all of these leading people, there was a man who worked --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Mrs. Pandurevic --

utterances.speaker: RADOJKA PANDUREVIC
utterances.text: -- on military records in the municipality -- well, I'm trying to explain to you that it had already been a long time that we had stopped this work and that we had established a council of sorts where we tried to see what we were to do next, and then we would try to explain to the Serb people by placing a notice in the paper on what it was that we were going to do.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: When did the Assembly of the Serbian Municipality of Hadzici get formed then?

utterances.speaker: RADOJKA PANDUREVIC
utterances.text: It was established in 1991, at the end of 1991, and it ceased to exist in -- or actually, it ceased to exist, it stopped working in October 1991, so it was very brief period that it was operational. Sometime between December 1990 up until early October 1991.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: You're saying that the Assembly of the Serbian Municipality of Hadzici stopped functioning in October 1991? That's what I understood from the interpretation.

utterances.speaker: RADOJKA PANDUREVIC
utterances.text: No, not the Serb municipality, but the Hadzici municipality of Bosnia and Herzegovina, of the then-Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: My question is about --

utterances.speaker: RADOJKA PANDUREVIC
utterances.text: And the Serbian Municipality of Hadzici had not been established yet. As you may know, it was only established sometime in April 1992. In other words, five months after the work of the Municipal Assembly of Hadzici ceased to function, of the former BH.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And two weeks after Dr. Karadzic made that statement at the Bosnian Serb Assembly?

utterances.speaker: RADOJKA PANDUREVIC
utterances.text: I don't remember that statement and I did not take part in the establishment of this Serb municipality. As you know, I could not attend because of the trip that I had to make.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm just going to go over to one last area. You refer in your statement at paragraph 65 to Muslims leaving Hadzici in the direction of Kiseljak because they were afraid of Serbian revenge. And you say you heard that from some friends. Did you hear that from Muslim friends?

utterances.speaker: RADOJKA PANDUREVIC
utterances.text: Both from Muslim and from Serb friends because horrible things were happening in Tarcin camp and those colleagues of theirs, their countrymen, they did those things to us, Serbs. And for this reason --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, Mrs. Pandurevic --

utterances.speaker: RADOJKA PANDUREVIC
utterances.text: -- they didn't feel safe and they tried to cross over.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
